title: 6 Best Mold Killers in 2026: Kill, Clean or Prevent Regrowth

description: RMR-141 is the best mold killer for most indoor jobs, with a bleach-free formula and about 10 minutes of wet contact. 6 picks for walls, grout and siding.

intro: The best mold killer for most indoor jobs is RMR-141, a bleach-free, EPA-registered fungicide that works on drywall, wood and concrete when the surface stays wet for about 10 minutes. For shower grout, a bleach spray such as Tilex or RMR-86 does the kill and the stain in one pass.

No single bottle handles every surface, so this guide ranks six products by the job each one does best: killing growth, lifting stains, preventing regrowth, working in a bedroom, or cleaning siding and roofs. You will also find how to read a label, what gear to wear, a step-by-step cleanup and the point where a pro should take over.
quickAnswer: Buy RMR-141 to kill mold on walls, wood and concrete without bleach damage, and keep it wet for the label contact time. Use Tilex or RMR-86 on grout and tile, Concrobium to keep regrowth away, Benefect Decon 30 in nurseries and bedrooms, and Wet and Forget outdoors. Fix the moisture first, or any product will fail.

blocks.p: The products on a mold aisle do three different jobs. Fungicides kill the living organism, stain removers clear the pigment that dead mold leaves behind, and inhibitors make a clean surface harder for new spores to colonize. Most rooms need two of those three, and the surface decides which two.
Only a product with an EPA registration number on the label may legally claim to kill mold. Check for that number before you trust any kill claim, then follow the contact time to the minute.

sections.h: The 6 Best Mold Killers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: These picks are ranked on EPA registration where it applies, the active ingredient, the contact time on the label, the range of surfaces each maker approves, the hazards on the safety data sheet and recurring patterns in owner reviews. None of them was put through lab trials for this guide, so every performance claim below comes from a label, a maker or owner reports.

blocks.h3: Best Overall Mold Killer: RMR-141 RTU Mold Killer and Disinfectant

blocks.p: RMR-141 is a ready-to-use spray built on quaternary ammonium compounds, the same chemistry family found in many hospital disinfectants. It carries an EPA registration with fungicidal claims, which means its kill statements were reviewed rather than simply printed on the bottle. The directions are short: soak the surface, keep it visibly wet for the stated contact time (about 10 minutes for mold), then wipe or let it air dry. Most disappointing results trace back to wiping early.

Because there is no chlorine in it, RMR-141 will not whiten fabric or etch most finishes, and the safety data sheet reads far milder than a bleach product's. The maker approves it for a long list of porous and nonporous surfaces, including drywall, wood and concrete. Its one weakness is cosmetic. Dead mold often leaves gray or black blotches that a quat will not lift, which is why the same company sells a separate stain remover.
**Pros:** EPA-registered fungicide; no bleach, no mixing, no rinse; approved for porous surfaces; low odor.
**Cons:** leaves staining behind; the surface must stay wet for the full contact time.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RMR-141+RTU+mold+killer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Stain Remover: RMR-86 Instant Mold Stain Remover

blocks.p: RMR-86 is the cleanup half of the RMR pair. Where RMR-141 kills, RMR-86 is designed to make the dark marks vanish, and owners describe the effect on shower grout, caulk lines and painted concrete as close to instant. The formula combines bleach with surfactants, so it hangs on vertical grout lines instead of running straight to the floor the way a homemade bleach solution does.

Use it after a fungicide on surfaces where the kill matters, or on its own for routine bathroom mildew. The trade-offs are the usual bleach ones: strong fumes that call for an open window and a running exhaust fan, damage to towels, carpet and colored finishes, and a hard rule against mixing it with ammonia, vinegar or any acid cleaner. Spot-test colored grout first.
**Pros:** clears dark mildew stains in seconds on many surfaces; clings to grout; little scrubbing; widely sold.
**Cons:** bleach fumes and fabric risk; not a substitute for a fungicide on porous materials.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RMR-86+instant+mold+stain+remover&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Prevention: Concrobium Mold Control

blocks.p: Concrobium works differently from bleach and quat sprays. Its actives are inorganic salts, and the maker says the liquid dries into a thin film that crushes existing growth and then keeps resisting new growth on that surface. It contains no bleach, ammonia or added VOCs according to the maker, so it is easy to use in an occupied home, and it is approved for wood, drywall, concrete, fabric and many other materials.

Coverage is the reason to buy it. Concrobium comes in gallon jugs as well as spray bottles and supports fogging, which turns a roof deck, a crawlspace full of joists or a whole basement after a water event into a practical job. Remediation contractors often apply it as the final step after cleaning. It does not remove staining, so pair it with a stain remover wherever appearance matters.
**Pros:** no bleach or ammonia; residual film resists regrowth; can be fogged over large areas; little odor.
**Cons:** leaves old stains in place; fogging needs a bought or rented fogger.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Concrobium+Mold+Control&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Showers and Tile: Tilex Mold and Mildew Remover

blocks.p: For pink and black mildew on tub caulk, tile grout and vinyl window frames, a bathroom bleach spray is the right tool, and Tilex from Clorox is the easiest one to find. It is EPA-registered, and its label claims it kills mold and mildew on hard nonporous surfaces while removing the stains, which covers almost every bathroom job and most window sills.

The spray foams slightly and stays on vertical tile long enough to work. Owners commonly report that light grout staining disappears after a few minutes and a rinse. Run the exhaust fan, crack a window and keep it away from colored bath mats. It is the wrong product for drywall, wood trim or a ceiling, where bleach can lighten the surface without reaching growth inside the material.
**Pros:** EPA-registered kill claims on hard surfaces; lifts grout stains with little scrubbing; foaming spray clings; sold almost everywhere.
**Cons:** strong fumes in small rooms; not for wood, drywall or other porous materials.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Tilex+Mold+and+Mildew+Remover&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Low-Toxicity Option: Benefect Botanical Decon 30

blocks.p: Benefect Decon 30 is the product remediation contractors often pick when people are living in the home and someone reacts badly to harsh chemicals. Its active ingredient is thymol, a compound from thyme oil, and it is registered with the EPA as a disinfectant. The safety data sheet lists far fewer hazards than bleach or concentrated quats, there is no chlorine smell, and most surfaces need no rinse.

That profile suits nurseries, bedrooms and any room people will use again within the hour. Botanical does not mean instant, so follow the label contact time as you would with any registered product. Like the other non-bleach picks, it leaves dark staining behind, and it costs more per ounce than mass-market sprays, so a quat or Concrobium makes more sense on large areas.
**Pros:** thymol active; EPA-registered disinfectant; low hazard profile; mild herbal smell; no rinse on most surfaces.
**Cons:** more expensive per ounce; does not remove stains.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Benefect+Botanical+Decon+30&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Exterior Surfaces: Wet and Forget Outdoor

blocks.p: Wet and Forget runs on a slower clock. You dilute the concentrate, spray it on siding, a roof, a deck, a fence or concrete, and walk away. Over the following weeks and months, sun, wind and rain wash the dead growth off without scrubbing or a pressure washer. That matters on cedar shingles, soft deck boards and roofs nobody wants to climb twice.

The active ingredient is a quaternary ammonium compound rather than bleach, which is gentler on paint and plants, although the maker still says to keep it off plantings while spraying and out of ponds. Owners are mostly happy with the end result and mostly frustrated by the wait: heavy black streaks can take a full season to fade. The maker says a single treatment can keep growth off for a year or more.
**Pros:** no scrubbing or pressure washing; approved for roofs, siding, decks and concrete; bleach-free; concentrate covers a large area.
**Cons:** results take weeks to months; must be kept off plants and out of water.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Wet+and+Forget+Outdoor+Cleaner+Concentrate&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: What Is the Difference Between Killing, Cleaning and Preventing Mold?

blocks.p: Killing stops the organism, cleaning removes the mark it leaves, and preventing makes the surface less welcoming next time. Each job takes a different product, and knowing which one you are doing stops you buying the wrong bottle.

blocks.h3: Killing needs a registered fungicide and time

blocks.p: A fungicide has to sit on the growth long enough to destroy it. In the U.S., only products with an EPA registration number may claim to kill mold, and their directions list a contact time, usually several minutes with the surface kept wet. The registered actives you will see most often are quaternary ammonium compounds, chlorine bleach, hydrogen peroxide and thymol.

Dead mold keeps its color. On grout, wood and painted concrete, that pigment stays as gray or black patches long after the organism has died. Bleach is the best stain lifter, which is why most bathroom sprays use it. The catch: a bleach stain remover used alone on porous material can whiten the surface while growth deeper inside survives.

blocks.h3: Preventing means a harder surface to colonize

blocks.p: Inhibitors such as Concrobium dry into a residue that discourages new growth. Some disinfectants also claim residual activity. Even so, no coating beats a dry surface. A treated wall that stays damp will grow mold again; an untreated wall that stays dry usually will not.

sections.h: Which Mold Killer Works Best on Walls, Wood, Grout and Windows?

blocks.p: The more porous the material, the more the product choice matters, and past a point the material has to be removed instead of cleaned. Sort your surface into one of these groups.

blocks.h3: Tile, grout, glass and window frames

blocks.p: Glazed tile, glass, vinyl window frames, plastic and metal are the easy case. Mold sits on top, nearly any registered product kills it, and a wipe takes the residue away. Bleach sprays like Tilex shine here because they handle the stain at the same time. For the black film in window tracks and on sills, spray, wait the label time, then scrub the corners with an old toothbrush. Window mold is almost always condensation, so the long-term fix is less indoor humidity, not a stronger spray.
Grout is slightly porous, so expect to repeat the treatment once on old, deeply stained lines. If staining returns quickly after the second round, the grout or caulk itself may need replacing.

blocks.h3: Painted drywall, sealed trim and concrete walls

blocks.p: These semi-porous surfaces need a product approved for them, plus patience. Mold can push its threadlike hyphae into paint films and the top layer of concrete. A non-bleach fungicide that soaks in, followed by a soft brush, usually beats bleach, which can whiten the surface while growth survives just under it. This is the most common job for RMR-141.

blocks.h3: Bare drywall, ceiling tile, carpet and insulation

blocks.p: Porous materials with significant growth often cannot be saved. The EPA advises that such materials may need to be discarded because growth inside them cannot be fully removed. Small surface spots on drywall can be cleaned, but if the paper face is soft, stained through or crumbling, cut the panel out at least a foot beyond the visible growth and replace it.

Framing falls between the two. Surface mold on studs and joists can usually be killed, cleaned and treated, with light sanding afterward if the staining bothers you. Sand only after the fungicide has done its work, never before. Wood that is soft or crumbly has rot as well as mold and needs repair. Once clean, keep framing below about 16 percent moisture content, checked with a pin meter, and it will not support new growth.

sections.h: Does Bleach, Vinegar or Hydrogen Peroxide Kill Mold?

blocks.p: Bleach kills mold on hard, nonporous surfaces. Vinegar and drugstore peroxide have some antifungal effect but carry no mold-killing registration, so treat them as backups for light mildew rather than a real treatment.

Bleach is excellent on tile and glass and unmatched at lifting stains. On wood and drywall it underperforms. Household bleach is mostly water, so the chlorine tends to react at the surface while the water soaks in, which can lighten the stain and leave growth underneath. The EPA does not generally recommend bleach for routine mold cleanup, noting that some spores survive and that the fumes are hazardous.

Distilled white vinegar is about 5 percent acetic acid. Studies show it inhibits some common household molds and does less against others. It is cheap and low-hazard, so it is fine for light mildew on a hard surface, but it is not registered, and results vary by species and surface. Never use it with bleach, because the combination releases chlorine gas.

The 3 percent peroxide sold in pharmacies also has antifungal activity and leaves no toxic residue, though it can lighten some materials. Spray, wait about 10 minutes, scrub and wipe. Like vinegar, it carries no mold label claim.

blocks.h3: Baking soda, borax and essential oils

blocks.p: Borax and baking soda help with scrubbing and leave a mildly alkaline film. Tea tree oil and other essential oils show antifungal activity in lab work, but they can irritate sensitive people and they are not registered products. On a real mold problem, use something with an EPA number.

Bleach plus ammonia gives off chloramine vapor, and bleach plus vinegar or another acid gives off chlorine gas. That includes two cleaners applied back to back on the same spot. Use one product per session, rinse before switching, and keep air moving out of the room.

sections.h: How Do You Read a Mold Killer Label?

blocks.p: Check four things, in this order: the EPA registration number, the contact time, the approved surfaces and the precautions. Together they tell you whether the product kills, how long it needs, where it belongs and how to stay safe.

Look for "EPA Reg. No." followed by digits, usually near the ingredient list. A registered product may claim to kill the organisms its label names. An unregistered one may clean, remove stains or deodorize, but it cannot legally claim to kill mold. That does not make it useless; it tells you which job it was designed for.

This is how long the surface must stay wet for the kill claim to hold. For mold, 10 minutes is common. On a wall or ceiling, staying wet usually means a spray, a few minutes, and a second spray before the first dries.

Every label lists where the product may go: hard nonporous surfaces only, or porous materials such as wood and drywall too. Using a nonporous-only product on wood voids its claims and can bleach or damage the material.

blocks.h3: The precautions and safety data sheet

blocks.p: The precautionary statements and the safety data sheet, which most makers post online, list the gloves, eye protection and ventilation the job needs and the products that must never be mixed with it. Bleach products carry stronger warnings than quats or thymol, and in a small room you will notice the difference.

sections.h: What Gear Do You Need to Remove Mold Safely?

blocks.p: For a small DIY cleanup, EPA guidance sets the minimum at an N-95 respirator, gloves that reach the middle of the forearm and goggles without vent holes. Scrubbing mold throws spores and fragments into the air, and a plain dust mask does not filter them well enough. Add long sleeves and clothes you can wash right after.

Put a box fan in an open window blowing outward so contaminated air leaves the house. Close interior doors and shut off the furnace or central air so return ducts do not pull spores into the system. A HEPA air purifier running nearby catches what escapes.
In a windowless bathroom, run the exhaust fan, take breaks and stop if your eyes or throat burn. Anyone with asthma or another lung condition should hand the job to someone else.

blocks.h3: Bag debris and clean up after

blocks.p: Bag cut-out drywall, insulation and rags inside the work area, seal the bags there, then carry them out. Wash your clothes, shower, and vacuum the area with a HEPA vacuum, since a standard vacuum can blow fine particles back into the room.

sections.h: How Do You Remove Mold Step by Step?

blocks.p: Fix the water, set up the room, kill, clean, then dry and treat. Skipping the first step is the main reason cleanups fail.

Find and fix the leak, condensation or seepage that fed the growth, then dry the area. In a basement, a unit from our [basement dehumidifier picks](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) set to 50 percent usually brings the space down within a couple of weeks. If water is coming through the walls, read our guide to [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) before you clean anything.

Put on the respirator, gloves and goggles, close the room off, start the window fan and lay plastic on the floor if debris will fall. Lightly mist the moldy area with water or the product so spores stay put.
Apply the registered fungicide until the surface is wet and keep it wet for the label time, reapplying on vertical surfaces. Never dry-brush or sand mold before treating it.
After the contact time, scrub with a soft brush or cloth and wipe the residue away. Use a stain remover on surfaces that can take it. Bag anything that cannot be cleaned.

Dry everything within 24 to 48 hours with fans and a dehumidifier, then apply an inhibitor such as Concrobium. Prime and paint only after the surface is dry and treated, using a mold-resistant primer where it fits. On basement block, our guide to the [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) covers coatings that also resist moisture.

sections.h: How Do You Get Rid of Mold and Mildew Outside?

blocks.p: Outdoors, use a leave-on treatment like Wet and Forget if you can wait, or a sprayed cleaner and a soft brush if you cannot, and keep both away from plants and water. The green, black or gray film on siding, decks, fences and roofs is usually a mix of mildew, algae and sometimes lichen, and it loves shaded, north-facing surfaces that stay damp.

The fast route is a pump-sprayer cleaner, often oxygen bleach or chlorine based, finished with a soft brush or a low-pressure rinse. The slow route is a leave-on product that keeps working every time it rains. On soft wood and asphalt shingles the slow route is safer, since aggressive pressure washing tears wood fibers and strips shingle granules.

A clean deck left bare in a shady yard will grow mildew again within a season or two. Let the wood dry completely, then protect it with a finish that contains a mildewcide. Our [deck stain reviews](/best-deck-stain-reviews/) cover formulas built for shady, damp yards.

Soak nearby plants before and after spraying, cover delicate beds and skip windy days. Bleach washes can scorch foliage and kill grass along the drip line, and even gentler quat products must stay out of ponds and streams.

sections.h: How Do You Keep Mold From Coming Back?

blocks.p: Hold relative humidity under about 50 percent and keep surfaces dry. That one change matters more than any product, because mold growth slows sharply under those conditions.

blocks.h3: Run a dehumidifier and an exhaust fan

blocks.p: In a basement, that usually means a dehumidifier running through the humid months. In a bathroom, it means an exhaust fan vented outdoors and left on for at least 20 minutes after each shower.

A slow drip under a sink, sweating cold-water pipes, a dryer venting indoors and a downspout dumping beside the foundation each create a damp pocket. Insulate cold pipes, extend downspouts 4 to 6 feet from the house and seal damp walls; our [basement wall sealer guide](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) covers products for that last step.

blocks.h3: Treat surfaces that cannot stay perfectly dry

blocks.p: Basement framing, roof decks and crawlspace joists benefit from an inhibitor after cleaning. When you repaint a bathroom or basement, use a mold-resistant primer and paint. Painting over live mold only hides it.
Pull furniture a few inches off cold exterior walls, store basement items in plastic bins instead of cardboard, and leave closet doors cracked in humid months.

sections.h: When Should You Call a Professional for Mold?

blocks.p: Call a professional when the moldy area is bigger than about 10 square feet, when growth is inside the ductwork or followed sewage, or when someone in the home is medically vulnerable. Larger jobs need containment barriers, negative air pressure and careful material removal to stop spores spreading through the house.

blocks.h3: Jobs that need a pro at any size

blocks.p: Mold in HVAC ducts gets blown through the whole home whenever the system runs. Growth after a sewage backup or floodwater carries health risks beyond the mold. A persistent musty smell with no visible source points to hidden growth that needs moisture meters and sometimes opened walls.

blocks.h3: How to hire a mold contractor

blocks.p: Pick a contractor who finds and fixes the moisture source, writes down the containment and removal plan, and does not lead with expensive air testing or fogging as the main fix. Ask about IICRC certification, read reviews and get at least two quotes. A good one will also tell you when a job is small enough to do yourself.

mistakes: Wiping Before the Contact Time Is Up

A registered fungicide only works while the surface stays wet for the label time, often around 10 minutes. Spray and wipe at once and you move some growth around but leave living mold behind. Wet it, wait, rewet any area that starts drying, and scrub only after the full time has passed.
Using Bleach on Drywall and Bare Wood

On porous materials, bleach lightens the surface while its water soaks deeper, where growth can survive and return, and it can weaken the drywall face. Use a non-bleach fungicide approved for porous surfaces, and replace drywall that is soft or stained all the way through.
Mixing Cleaners or Using Them Back to Back

Bleach with ammonia releases chloramine vapor, and bleach with vinegar or another acid releases chlorine gas. It often happens when two products go on the same spot minutes apart. Use one product per session, rinse the surface, and ventilate before switching.

No paint or primer kills established mold, including mold-resistant formulas. A fresh coat hides the stain for a few months while the growth continues underneath until it bleeds through or lifts the film. Kill, clean, dry and treat first, then prime.

A spotless wall grows mold again if the leak, condensation or high humidity behind it remains. Find and stop the water first, then keep humidity under about 50 percent with a dehumidifier, an exhaust fan or better airflow in the room.
bottomLine: For most indoor mold, RMR-141 is the bottle to buy: it kills growth on walls, framing and concrete without the damage bleach can cause, as long as you keep the surface wet for the full contact time. Add RMR-86 or Tilex where stains on grout and tile need to disappear, Concrobium to keep regrowth off wood and drywall, Benefect Decon 30 for rooms where children or sensitive people sleep, and Wet and Forget for siding, roofs and decks. None of them will last if the area stays damp, so fix the water first, hold humidity under 50 percent, and call a professional for anything larger than about 10 square feet, anything in the ducts and anything that followed sewage.

faqs.q: What is the best mold killer?
faqs.a: RMR-141 is the best mold killer for most indoor jobs. It is an EPA-registered, bleach-free quat fungicide approved for drywall, wood and concrete, and it works when the surface stays wet for about 10 minutes. For shower grout and tile, a registered bleach spray like Tilex kills the mold and removes the stain at the same time.

faqs.q: What is the best mold remover for the bathroom?
faqs.a: Tilex Mold and Mildew Remover is the easiest strong choice for bathroom tile, grout and caulk, because it is EPA-registered for hard surfaces and lifts stains in one pass. RMR-86 works faster on stubborn grout stains. Run the exhaust fan, open a window and never use either one right after an ammonia or acid cleaner.

Any EPA-registered fungicide whose label lists mold kills so-called black mold, since the color does not change the treatment. RMR-141 suits walls and wood, while Tilex suits tile and glass. Keep the surface wet for the full contact time. Large patches, over about 10 square feet, should go to a professional.

faqs.q: What is the best mold remover for grout?
faqs.a: A bleach-based remover such as RMR-86 or Tilex is best for grout, because grout stains need bleach to disappear and these sprays cling to vertical lines. Spray, wait the label time, scrub with a stiff toothbrush and rinse. If black spots return within weeks, the grout or caulk may need replacing.

faqs.q: What kills mold on porous surfaces?
faqs.a: A non-bleach fungicide approved for porous materials, such as RMR-141 or Benefect Decon 30, works best on wood and painted drywall because it soaks in rather than just whitening the surface. Keep it wet for the label time and scrub gently. Heavily moldy carpet, ceiling tile and soft drywall usually need to be removed.

faqs.q: What is the best mold killer for windows?
faqs.a: Tilex or another registered bleach spray works well on glass, vinyl frames and sills, since they are nonporous. Use RMR-141 on painted wood trim instead. Spray, wait, scrub the corners and dry everything. Window mold comes from condensation, so lowering indoor humidity is the real long-term fix.

faqs.q: How do you keep mold from coming back after removal?
faqs.a: Keep humidity below about 50 percent and stop every water source; that matters more than any product. Run a dehumidifier in damp basements, use a bathroom exhaust fan for 20 minutes after showers, and apply an inhibitor like Concrobium to framing or drywall after cleaning. Recurring growth in one spot means an unfixed leak.
